directAnswer: Pope St. Martin I reigned from 649 to 655. He convened the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned Monothelitism and the emperor's decree forbidding debate on Christ's two wills; for this he was arrested by imperial agents, tried in Constantinople, and exiled to Crimea, where he died. He is the last pope venerated as a martyr.

sections.h2: From Todi to the Throne of Peter
paras: Martin was born near Todi in Umbria. Before his election he served as papal envoy to Constantinople, which gave him firsthand knowledge of the court and of the Christological disputes there. Elected after Theodore I's death in 649, he was consecrated in July without waiting for confirmation from Emperor Constans II, a step that Constantinople treated as defiance.

In October 649 Martin opened a council at the Lateran Basilica attended by about 105 bishops, mostly from Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, and North Africa, along with Greek monks living in Rome; the thought of Maximus the Confessor deeply shaped its work. The council taught that Christ, being fully God and fully man, has two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, united without confusion or division.

It condemned Monothelitism and anathematized its leading proponents, including Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul of Constantinople. It also rejected both the Ekthesis of Heraclius and the Typos of Constans II. Martin sent the decrees throughout the West and to the East, and the emperor regarded the council as an open challenge to his authority.

sections.h2: Arrest, Trial, and Exile to Crimea
paras: Constans II first ordered the exarch Olympius to arrest the pope, but Olympius instead came to terms with Martin and later rebelled against the emperor. In June 653 a new exarch, Theodore Calliopas, seized Martin, who was ill, in the Lateran and sent him by sea to Constantinople. After a long journey that included a stay on the island of Naxos, he arrived in the capital and was held in prison for months.

He was tried not for doctrine but for treason, accused of supporting Olympius. Condemned, he was publicly stripped of his insignia and paraded through the city. The dying patriarch Paul II is reported to have asked the emperor to spare his life, and the death sentence was changed to exile. Martin was sent to Cherson in Crimea, where his surviving letters describe hunger, illness, and a sense of abandonment. He died there on 16 September 655.

While Martin was still alive in exile, the Roman clergy, under imperial pressure, elected Eugene I in 654; Martin appears to have accepted the arrangement. After his death he was honored in both East and West as a martyr for the faith, and he is the last pope the Church venerates as such. The teaching he defended was vindicated by the Third Council of Constantinople in 680–681. In the General Roman Calendar his memorial is April 13; before the 1969 reform it was kept on November 12. Eastern Churches also commemorate him.

keyFacts: Born near Todi, Umbria; former papal envoy to Constantinople
Convened the Lateran Council of October 649 against Monothelitism
Arrested in 653, tried in Constantinople, exiled to Cherson in Crimea
Last pope venerated as a martyr; memorial April 13 (formerly November 12)

faqs.question: Why was Pope Martin I arrested?
faqs.answer: He convened the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned the emperor's Typos and the Monothelite teaching it protected. Constans II had him seized in 653, and in Constantinople he was formally charged with treason rather than with any doctrinal error.

faqs.question: Where did Pope St. Martin I die?
faqs.answer: He died in exile at Cherson, an imperial outpost on the Crimean peninsula, in September 655, worn down by hunger and illness.

faqs.question: Why is Martin I considered a martyr?
faqs.answer: He died in exile as a result of persecution for defending the Church's teaching that Christ has a human and a divine will. The Church honors him as a martyr, and he is the most recent pope to receive that title.
